name: Pancho Villa
role: Mexican revolutionary commander and provisional governor of Chihuahua (1913–1914)
summary: Villa fought in the Mexican Revolution and led the División del Norte. In Chihuahua he confiscated estates from powerful landowners. His 1915 agrarian law called for state governments to break up large holdings and transfer plots to cultivators.

sources.title: Ley General Agraria, 24 May 1915
sources.usedFor: Land ceilings, purchase and cultivation of smallholdings, state implementation, and federal oversight.

sources.title: Decrees establishing the Bank of the State of Chihuahua and confiscating property, 12 December 1913
sources.usedFor: Villa’s own banking and confiscation decrees, reproduced from the official gazette.

sources.title: Manifiesto de Francisco Villa al pueblo mexicano, 22 September 1914
sources.usedFor: Popular legitimacy, constitutional restoration and the proposed interim government.

sources.title: John Reed, México insurgente (Spanish edition, Memoria Política de México)
sources.usedFor: Contemporary account of Villa’s price orders, currency, expropriations, public services and expulsions.

sources.title: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1915, document 837, enclosure 3
sources.usedFor: Villa’s decree assuming emergency political authority and establishing departments.

sources.title: Library of Congress, Civil War: Conventionist Viewpoint
sources.usedFor: Villa’s governing record, use of force and agrarian measures.

sources.title: Villa’s San Andrés manifesto, December 1916 (U.S. consular translation)
sources.usedFor: Direct presidential elections, legislative checks, foreign property and nationalization, compulsory mobilization, and opposition to the U.S. expedition.

sources.title: U.S. consular report on treatment of Catholic institutions in Chihuahua, 26 January 1915
sources.usedFor: Report of Villa’s expulsion of Paulist monks, closure of their seminary, and demands on clergy.

sources.title: Memórica, Pacto de Sabinas
sources.usedFor: Terms under which Villa disarmed his forces and made peace with the interim government.

sources.title: John Reed, México insurgente, chapter El lado humano (Spanish edition, Memoria Política de México)
sources.usedFor: Reed’s extended conversation with Villa about political rights for women.

sources.title: Regino Hernández Llergo, Una semana con Villa en Canutillo (Universidad de Colima edition, Scribd mirror)
sources.usedFor: Full 1922 interview, including Villa’s remarks on class equality, elections and religion.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Villa retained a military command under the Convention government. In the Sabinas agreement he disarmed his own force and arranged a federally paid military escort.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: Villa’s law required states to sell redistributed plots and protected smallholdings as inheritable family property.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: Villa’s 1916 manifesto called on Mexicans to take up arms and oust Pershing’s expedition, which he held had invaded and occupied Mexican territory with Carranza’s acquiescence.

civilians-legitimate-targets.rationale: The Library of Congress records that Villa ordered attacks on captured women in Namiquipa in retaliation for an officer’s betrayal during his campaign against Carranza.

collective-farming.rationale: Villa’s agrarian law divided estates into individually worked holdings and set aside only shared woods, grazing and watering places for those plot holders.

conscription.rationale: Article XIV of Villa’s 1916 programme directed military leaders to mobilize the population and threatened confiscation for anyone who refused to take part against the U.S. incursion.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Villa’s September 1914 manifesto held that Mexicans would recognize only governments deriving their authority from the popular will and called for restoring constitutional government by elections.

death-penalty.rationale: In Chihuahua Villa prescribed execution as punishment for offenses including theft and the sale of alcohol to troops. Reed reports that a soldier was executed for drunkenness.

decide-locally.rationale: Villa’s agrarian law expressly limited federal rules to general principles and assigned ceilings, adjudication and implementation to state governments on the grounds that local needs differed and central execution would delay reform.

direct-action.rationale: Villa’s 1914 manifesto called for armed resistance to restore elected constitutional government. His 1916 platform assigned the highest priority to popular elections for president.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Article I of Villa’s San Andrés platform called for voters themselves to elect the president by free suffrage, including votes cast by military personnel.

economic-freedom.rationale: In promulgating the 1915 law, Villa identified dependence on a small landowning class as preventing wage laborers from freely exercising their civil and political rights.

elective-rulers.rationale: Villa called for electing a constitutional president in 1914 and made electing the president by unrestricted suffrage the first article of his 1916 platform.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: During the revolution Villa held Luis Terrazas as a hostage and summarily confiscated the assets of families he identified as backing his opponents, leaving their legal liability to be determined afterward.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Villa’s expulsion order applied to Spaniards in Chihuahua on the basis of their nationality and threatened execution for remaining in the state.

equal-outcomes.rationale: In the Canutillo interview Villa explicitly rejected equalizing the social classes and defended a society in which people occupy different economic positions and can improve their standing through their work.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Villa’s 1916 platform barred real-estate purchases by foreign nationals, with a narrow exception tied to long-standing naturalization and continuous residence.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: The agrarian law’s preamble held that economic dependence on a small landowning class itself kept rural laborers from exercising their civil and political rights freely.

land-redistribution.rationale: Articles 1–3 and 12–14 of Villa’s agrarian law required the breakup of oversized estates and gave sharecroppers preference for plots they had cultivated.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Reed describes Villa putting the city waterworks, electricity plant, streetcars and telephone under direct public administration upon taking office.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Villa’s San Andrés manifesto praised Mexicans who gave their lives resisting invasion as having earned lasting national honor.

money-backed-by-precious-metals.rationale: Villa ordered the state bank to back paper issues peso for peso with gold and copper coin. His emergency paper issue circulated on his authority alone and his administration compelled merchants to accept it.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Villa tasked government with reorganizing farmland ownership, maintaining irrigation and rural transport, and financing agricultural credit.

opposition-only-legal-channels.rationale: Villa led an armed rebellion against Huerta and continued fighting against Carranza after the revolutionary coalition split.

population-transfer.rationale: Villa ordered Spaniards to leave Chihuahua on pain of death and treated the Spanish community as collectively implicated in support for his opponents.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: John Reed reports that Villa set maximum prices for beef, milk and bread when a shortage hit Chihuahua.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Villa’s bank decree singled out poor farmers for lending assistance. His administration used newly issued currency and staple price ceilings to restore food access during a shortage.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Villa assigned valuation disputes under his agrarian law to local judges and authorized federal tribunals to invalidate improper land transfers.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Villa detained Luis Terrazas as a hostage and conditioned his release on a ransom paid by his father, exercising power directly outside the ordinary courts.

property-franchise.rationale: Villa’s 1916 platform called for presidential suffrage without restrictions and encouraged voters to choose congressional representatives of humble origins.

property-fundamental.rationale: Villa confiscated property from named wealthy families in 1913 and imposed a statewide land-ceiling and compulsory purchase framework in his 1915 agrarian law.

public-ownership.rationale: Villa placed the electricity plant, waterworks, telephone and streetcars under direct military administration in Chihuahua, alongside mills and confiscated estates.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Villa commanded revolutionary forces against Huerta after the overthrow of the constitutional Madero government.

separate-church-state.rationale: Villa expelled Paulist monks and closed their seminary after taking Chihuahua. His military administration imposed special levies on priests and took over Catholic institutional property.

separated-powers.rationale: Villa’s 1916 programme assigned Congress the task of checking the president’s acts. In 1914 he condemned Carranza for absorbing all three constitutional powers.

state-harmful.rationale: Villa created civilian administrative departments to maintain public services and subsequently assigned state and federal governments permanent responsibilities in his agrarian law.

suppress-opposition.rationale: As military governor, Villa expelled political opponents, held Luis Terrazas hostage, and had some of the people identified as political enemies executed in the penitentiary.

torture-always-illegal.rationale: Reed reports that Villa personally used coercion amounting to torture on Luis Terrazas to make him reveal where the bank’s reserves were hidden.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Villa’s agrarian law identified concentrated landownership as a threat to political and civil liberty and to the stability of public institutions.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The 1915 law capped large estates and directed the states to sell the land they expropriated as small plots on favorable terms.

women-distinct-values.rationale: In the same conversation Villa described women as particularly compassionate and said that a woman would be reluctant to order someone executed.

women-suffrage.rationale: Villa initially doubted that women would vote. After Reed explained that women voted in the United States, Villa said he saw no reason they could not do so in Mexico, while expressing doubts about their judgment.

notes: Reviewed economy, government, society, world affairs, liberty, culture, ecology, technology, means and globalism against Villa’s decrees, manifestos, negotiations and contemporary accounts. Follow-up focused on church and state, women’s political rights, federal and local authority, restrictions on foreigners, trade and intervention. Villa shifted from wartime trade with the United States to calling for a bilateral trade suspension and resistance to the U.S. expedition in 1916. The 1920 Sabinas settlement ended his military campaign.
